clue.text: English vehicle, one with another about to block this, the height of danger in Italy

definitions.text: the height of danger in Italy

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters are written backwards
a blocking piece sits inside a passage and fills it, so one string is lodged within the other

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
a sports utility vehicle, the big four-wheel-drive car
I is the Roman numeral for one
a second vehicle of the same kind

explanation.surface: A tourist in a hired car hears another vehicle is about to cut off the road up the dangerous Italian peak.
explanation.walkthrough: SUV, a sports utility vehicle, is a common term in Britain and America alike. 'This' points the wordplay at the definition, and 'about' turns only the second vehicle, which then surrounds the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The volcano near Naples is a mountain, so a height, and one that famously threatens the towns around its slopes.

clue.text: Allowed to involve son in case

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in and include it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: let means allowed or permitted
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent permits a son to be brought into some matter or legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In case' reads like part of the surface story about involvement in a case, but it is the definition, a conjunction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are conjunctions introducing a precaution: you do something lest, or in case, a bad outcome happens.

clue.text: The Fellowship of the Ring

blocks.note: first meaning: a group of associates or friends
second meaning: a round shape or band

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is printed in italics as Tolkien's book title, but it splits into two separate meanings joined by 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A social set of friends is called a circle, and a ring is a circular shape, so one word covers both.

clue.text: Unhappy expressions of dejection said to reduce business

indicators.note: something said is spoken out, so these letters are chosen for how they sound rather than how they are spelt

blocks.note: feeling down is feeling unhappy
sighs are breaths that express sadness, and they sound the same as this spelling

explanation.surface: Gloomy groans in the office as the firm announces cutbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The sounds-alike applies only to the expressions of dejection: 'sighs' and SIZE are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: To downsize is to shrink a company, usually by cutting staff, so it is a verb for making a business smaller.

clue.text: Briefly village’s terrible rainfall drowning paying guest

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked out of order
in a down clue, something drowning another lies on top of it, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
PG is the abbreviation for a paying guest, a lodger

explanation.surface: A Welsh village endures awful rain that floods out a lodger.
explanation.walkthrough: Llanfairpwllgwyngyll on Anglesey, in Wales, has one of the world's longest place names, so it is usually shortened to LLANFAIR PG; 'Briefly' signals the short form.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the everyday abbreviated name used for the famously long-named Anglesey village, on road signs and railway timetables.

clue.text: Oust team’s wingers for new formation: that’s the limit!

indicators.note: wingers play on the flanks, so only the two edge letters of the word are kept
a new formation is a fresh arrangement of the players, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
the first and last letters of team

explanation.surface: A football manager drops the wide players and switches to a new formation, and a fan cries that it's the last straw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wingers' and 'formation' both look like football talk, but one picks the outer letters and the other rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: The utmost is the furthest extent or greatest degree possible, the point beyond which nothing more can go.

clue.text: Root cause to lose heart: crumbly eclair

indicators.note: losing the heart means the middle goes, leaving only the two outside letters
something crumbly falls into pieces, so these letters break up and re-form

blocks.note: the word with its inside removed
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A baker diagnoses why the éclair fell apart: the root cause was a weak centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Root cause' reads as one phrase, but 'Root' alone is the definition; 'cause' is the start of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Celeriac is a vegetable grown for its swollen, knobbly root, a form of celery.

clue.text: Roughly check about a reservation

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: ca. abbreviates circa, Latin for roughly
to vet is to check thoroughly
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone casually checks on a booking at a restaurant or hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reservation' suggests a booking, but here it is a doubt or proviso; the 'a' is used twice, once in the wordplay only.
explanation.definitionFit: A caveat is a warning or qualifying condition, and a reservation is likewise a doubt or qualification attached to agreement.

clue.text: Associate of monastery is not quite spherical

blocks.note: first meaning: a lay person attached to a religious community
second meaning: flattened at the poles, like the Earth

explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes about a rotund monk; the two halves are unrelated meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblate is a layperson dedicated to a monastic order, and an oblate spheroid is a sphere squashed at its poles.

clue.text: Almost entirely set free

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: quite can mean entirely or completely, as in quite right

explanation.surface: Someone has very nearly been released from captivity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost entirely' reads as a single adverbial phrase, but 'Almost' operates on the word for 'entirely'.
explanation.definitionFit: In an older sense, quit is an adjective meaning released or rid of, as in being quit of a debt.

clue.text: Leader of choir admits Baker, a sweary person

indicators.note: to admit is to let someone inside, so one piece is taken into another

blocks.note: a cantor leads the singing in a synagogue or church
an oven is something that bakes

explanation.surface: A choirmaster lets in someone called Baker, who turns out to curse a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes 'Baker' look like a surname, but it is the thing that bakes. 'Sweary' is used playfully to mean one who swears an oath, not one who curses.
explanation.definitionFit: A covenantor enters into a covenant, a solemn binding agreement, so is literally a person who swears to it.

clue.text: Thrill of subtle colour across lake

indicators.note: lying across something means spanning it on both sides, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: a tinge is a faint trace of colour
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: The pleasure of seeing a delicate hue spread over a lake at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across' looks like a direction for the colour spreading over the water, but it tells you the tinge wraps around the lake's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tingle is a prickling sensation of excitement, and a thrill is the same quick rush of feeling.

clue.text: Custodian, energetic type, hiding key on purpose

indicators.note: something hidden is tucked inside a covering, so the following material goes within

blocks.note: a goer is a lively, energetic person
the Alt key on a computer keyboard
an end is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: A dynamic caretaker deliberately conceals a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key on purpose' sounds like deliberately hiding a key, but 'on' just places the purpose after the key, and both go inside the energetic type.
explanation.definitionFit: Goaltender is the North American term, especially in ice hockey, for a goalkeeper, often called the custodian of the net.

clue.text: One tin and initially three beer bottles in Spanish resort

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
to bottle something is to hold it inside a vessel, so one piece encloses the others

blocks.note: ale is a kind of beer
I is the Roman numeral for one
a can is a tin
the opening letter of three

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker's shopping list on the Costa Blanca: a tin and three bottles of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun counted by 'three', but it is a verb: the beer holds the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Alicante is a port city and holiday destination on Spain's Costa Blanca, on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Give a hard look round very fast

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to stare is to look hard and fixedly
V is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Someone glances sharply around at great speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very fast' reads as one phrase meaning quickly, but 'very' belongs to the wordplay and 'fast' is a verb meaning go without food.
explanation.definitionFit: To fast is to go without eating, and to starve is likewise to go hungry, whether by choice or not.

clue.text: Green supporter pens joke, ultimately one of several in column

indicators.note: to pen an animal is to shut it inside an enclosure, so one piece encloses another
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: vert is green in heraldry, from the French
the final letter of joke
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: An environmental campaigner writes a punchline for one of a series of newspaper columns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' and 'column' suggest journalism, but 'pens' means encloses and the column is the spine.
explanation.definitionFit: The spinal column is made of a stack of small bones, each one a vertebra, so several are in it.

clue.text: Mastered Latin to gain respect at last

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Latin
to earn is to gain by effort
the final letter of respect

explanation.surface: A student masters Latin in the hope of finally being respected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' reads as finally gaining respect, but it picks only the closing letter of 'respect'. LEARNT is the usual British past tense of learn.
explanation.definitionFit: To have mastered a subject is to have learnt it thoroughly; both are past-tense verbs of acquiring knowledge or skill.

clue.text: Racist is doddery, of an age with the dinosaurs

definitions.text: of an age with the dinosaurs

indicators.note: a doddery person is shaky and unsteady, so these letters wobble out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An elderly bigot is shaky and so old-fashioned he might as well be a dinosaur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dinosaur' is slang for someone hopelessly outdated, which is how the surface uses it; the definition takes it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The Triassic is the geological period when dinosaurs first appeared, so the word describes rocks or creatures from that era.

clue.text: Beautiful-sounding woman and mother? A malicious old one

indicators.note: sounding refers to how a word is said, so the letters are chosen for their sound not their spelling

blocks.note: a belle is a beautiful woman, and this short spelling is said the same way
a dam is the mother of an animal, as in horse breeding

explanation.surface: A woman who seems lovely and maternal turns out to be a spiteful old crone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman' is part of the sounds-alike phrase, telling you the beautiful one is a belle; the definition's 'one' also means a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A beldam is an old-fashioned word for a hag, an ugly or spiteful old woman.

clue.text: In middle of long play perhaps catheter failed

definitions.text: In middle of long play perhaps

indicators.note: something that has failed has broken down, so these letters fall apart and re-form

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Halfway through a lengthy theatre performance, a patient's medical tube gives way.
explanation.walkthrough: A long play such as many of Shakespeare's has five acts, so the third falls in the middle; 'perhaps' admits the example.
explanation.definitionFit: In a five-act drama the third act is the central one, so it is a fair example of the middle of a long play.

clue.text: Owner of shell company with no time to be author

indicators.note: no means without, so the following letter is taken out

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
to be an author is to write
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: The head of a shell company has no time to write a book.
explanation.walkthrough: A shell company is a front with no real business, but here the shell is a real one on a sea snail.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowrie is a sea snail with a glossy, rounded shell, so it is the creature that owns such a shell.

clue.text: Speaking Italian today in the arcade

indicators.note: a thing placed in another sits within it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: la is the Italian feminine word for the; the clue's Italian setting covers it too
oggi is Italian for today

explanation.surface: Someone chatting in Italian in a shopping arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaking Italian' tells you both the words for 'today' and 'the' are in Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: A loggia is a gallery or arcade open on one side, a covered colonnade typical of Italian architecture.

clue.text: Left snake for its opposite

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
the adder is Britain's native venomous snake

explanation.surface: A snake was left in place of its opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: In the board game Snakes and Ladders a snake slides you down and a ladder lifts you up, so the ladder is the snake's opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladders carry players upward on the board while snakes carry them downward, making them the game's paired opposites.

clue.text: Incest took place in such a room?

definitions.text: Incest took place in such a room?

blocks.clueFragment: Incest took place in such a room?
blocks.note: surface reading: a lurid question about where a crime happened
setter's reading: a sibling sleeping with a sibling born at the same time, a pun on a hotel room with two single beds

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated answer describes a hotel room with two separate beds, but read literally it describes siblings born together having bedded each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotels describe a room with two single beds this way, and the literal sense of siblings sleeping together fits the scandal.

clue.text: Buzzer has become loud?

blocks.note: if something has become something else, it formerly was something different
p for piano means quiet in music; becoming loud implies it used to be quiet

explanation.surface: Someone notices a buzzing insect has got noisier.
explanation.walkthrough: The logic runs backwards: if it has become loud, it was quiet before, and P is the musical abbreviation for quiet. The question mark flags the twist.
explanation.definitionFit: A wasp is an insect that makes a buzzing noise in flight, so it is a fair, playful example of a buzzer.

clue.text: Global medical body comes to a halt

blocks.note: the World Health Organization
taken as written

explanation.surface: An international health agency grinds to a standstill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes to a halt' reads as one phrase; 'a' is wordplay, and only 'halt' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoa is the command used to make a horse stop, so it is a call meaning halt.

clue.text: Inability to recognise pitch in strip oddly missing close by

indicators.note: with the odd-numbered letters gone, only the even-numbered letters survive

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of strip
near means close by

explanation.surface: A footballer can't spot the pitch markings because some of the lines are missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' suggests a sports field, but it is musical pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a tin ear means being unable to hear musical tones accurately, a lack of ear for music.

clue.text: Richard Of York … for one was a jogger

blocks.note: first meaning: the start of a well-known memory aid for the colours of the rainbow
second meaning: something that jogs the memory

explanation.walkthrough: Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain gives red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. A jogger is not a runner here but something that jogs your memory.
explanation.definitionFit: A memory aid such as a rhyme or acronym prompts recall, so it is both an example phrase and a prompt for remembering.
